claim: Urodele amphibians and teleost fish possess the ability to regenerate injured complex structures such as limbs, fins, jaws, and heart by epimorphic regeneration.
source: Urodele amphibians and teleost fish are unique among vertebrates in that they possess the ability to regenerate injured complex structures such as limbs, fins, jaws, and heart by epimorphic regeneration (Morgan, 1901; Brockes and Kumar, 2008; Poss, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Morgan, 1901; Brockes and Kumar, 2008; Poss, 2010)

claim: Zebrafish fin regeneration proceeds through steps that include wound healing, blastema formation, and regenerative outgrowth to faithfully restore preinjury structures and size of the fin.
source: For example, zebrafish fin regeneration proceeds through steps that include wound healing, blastema formation, and regenerative outgrowth to faithfully restore preinjury structures and size of the fin (Poss et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poss et al., 2003

claim: In highly regenerative species, the blastema consists of a heterogeneous pool of highly proliferative mesenchymal cells that gives rise to the large amount of new tissue in the regenerate.
source: In such highly regenerative species, the blastema consists of a heterogeneous pool of highly proliferative mesenchymal cells that gives rise to the large amount of new tissue in the regenerate (Knopf et al., 2011; Tu and Johnson, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knopf et al., 2011 and Tu and Johnson, 2011

claim: Absence of a proliferative blastema is a prominent feature of most mammalian solid tissue injury responses.
source: In contrast, absence of a proliferative blastema is a prominent feature of most mammalian solid tissue injury responses (Muneoka et al., 2008; Straube and Tanaka, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Muneoka et al., 2008 and Straube and Tanaka, 2006

claim: Tumor suppressor genes control the proliferative and differentiated state of cells.
source: Tumor suppressor genes control the proliferative and differentiated state of cells, and many are also developmental regulators critical for normal formation of tissues (Jacks et al., 1992; Berman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jacks et al., 1992 and Berman et al., 2008

claim: Many tumor suppressor genes are developmental regulators critical for normal formation of tissues.
source: Tumor suppressor genes control the proliferative and differentiated state of cells, and many are also developmental regulators critical for normal formation of tissues (Jacks et al., 1992; Berman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jacks et al., 1992 and Berman et al., 2008

claim: The retinoblastoma gene Rb1 regulates the G1/S transition by sequestering E2f transcription factors.
source: For example, in eukaryotes the retinoblastoma gene Rb1 regulates the G1/S transition by sequestering E2f transcription factors, and it controls cellular differentiation by associating with chromatin modifiers to regulate activity of tissue-specific transcription factors.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about Rb1 function

claim: Rb1 controls cellular differentiation by associating with chromatin modifiers to regulate activity of tissue-specific transcription factors.
source: For example, in eukaryotes the retinoblastoma gene Rb1 regulates the G1/S transition by sequestering E2f transcription factors, and it controls cellular differentiation by associating with chromatin modifiers to regulate activity of tissue-specific transcription factors.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about Rb1 function

claim: The mammalian gene Cdkn2a is an essential tumor suppressor in mice and humans.
source: In contrast, the mammalian gene Cdkn2a is an essential tumor suppressor in mice and humans, but it is dispensable for mammalian development and tissue formation (Serrano et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Serrano et al., 1996

claim: Cdkn2a is dispensable for mammalian development and tissue formation.
source: In contrast, the mammalian gene Cdkn2a is an essential tumor suppressor in mice and humans, but it is dispensable for mammalian development and tissue formation (Serrano et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Serrano et al., 1996

claim: In mammals, Cdkn2a encodes two structurally unrelated proteins translated via alternate reading frames, p16Ink4a and Arf.
source: In mammals, Cdkn2a encodes two structurally unrelated proteins translated via alternate reading frames, p16Ink4a and Arf, each of which is a tumor suppressor (Chin et al., 1998; Sherr, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chin et al., 1998 and Sherr, 2006

claim: Both p16Ink4a and Arf are tumor suppressors.
source: In mammals, Cdkn2a encodes two structurally unrelated proteins translated via alternate reading frames, p16Ink4a and Arf, each of which is a tumor suppressor (Chin et al., 1998; Sherr, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chin et al., 1998 and Sherr, 2006

claim: p16Ink4a is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that functions upstream of Rb1.
source: While p16Ink4a is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor (CKI) that functions upstream of Rb1, Arf exerts its tumor suppressor function by responding to inappropriate Rb pathway signaling above a presumed threshold (Lowe and Sherr, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lowe and Sherr, 2003

claim: Arf exerts its tumor suppressor function by responding to inappropriate Rb pathway signaling above a presumed threshold.
source: While p16Ink4a is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor (CKI) that functions upstream of Rb1, Arf exerts its tumor suppressor function by responding to inappropriate Rb pathway signaling above a presumed threshold (Lowe and Sherr, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lowe and Sherr, 2003

claim: When induced, Arf stabilizes and activates Tp53 by binding and sequestering Mdm2.
source: When induced, it stabilizes and activates Tp53 by binding and sequestering Mdm2, an E3 ubiquitin ligase and negative regulator of Tp53 (Pomerantz et al., 1998; Weber et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pomerantz et al., 1998 and Weber et al., 1999

claim: Mdm2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase and negative regulator of Tp53.
source: When induced, it stabilizes and activates Tp53 by binding and sequestering Mdm2, an E3 ubiquitin ligase and negative regulator of Tp53 (Pomerantz et al., 1998; Weber et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pomerantz et al., 1998 and Weber et al., 1999

claim: Stabilized Tp53 either promotes cell cycle arrest or apoptosis depending on the context.
source: Depending on the context, stabilized Tp53 either promotes cell cycle arrest or apoptosis.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about Tp53 function

claim: Arf has functions including controlling ribosome biogenesis and responding to oxidative stress.
source: In addition to canonical Tp53-dependent functions, Arf has other important functions including controlling ribosome biogenesis and responding to oxidative stress (Sherr, 2006; Weber et al., 2000; Damalas et al., 2011; Menendez et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sherr, 2006; Weber et al., 2000; Damalas et al., 2011; Menendez et al., 2003

claim: The general function of Arf is to maintain the postmitotic state.
source: The resulting general function of Arf is to maintain the postmitotic state, and we have previously shown that suppression of Arf in the context of compromise of the Rb pathway results in dedifferentiation and proliferation of mammalian muscle cells in culture (Pajcini et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pajcini et al., 2010

claim: Suppression of Arf in the context of compromise of the Rb pathway results in dedifferentiation and proliferation of mammalian muscle cells in culture.
source: The resulting general function of Arf is to maintain the postmitotic state, and we have previously shown that suppression of Arf in the context of compromise of the Rb pathway results in dedifferentiation and proliferation of mammalian muscle cells in culture (Pajcini et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pajcini et al., 2010

claim: Regulation of Tp53 has been shown to be important during epimorphic regeneration, where it is downregulated during blastema formation.
source: Regulation of Tp53 has recently been shown to be important during epimorphic regeneration, where it is downregulated during blastema formation (Yun et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yun et al., 2013

claim: The advent of somatic stem cells in metazoans is thought to have enabled the formation of new types of cancer, thus requiring advanced tumor suppressor mechanisms.
source: The advent of somatic stem cells in metazoans is thought to have enabled the formation of new types of cancer, thus requiring advanced tumor suppressor mechanisms (Belyi et al., 2010; Pearson and Sanchez Alvarado, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Belyi et al., 2010 and Pearson and Sanchez Alvarado, 2008

claim: Arf is poorly conserved in non-mammalian lineages.
source: Although tumor suppressors are generally highly conserved in eukaryotes, Arf is unusual in that it is poorly conserved in non-mammalian lineages (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A showing phylogenetic comparison

claim: The Cdkn2a/b locus of teleost fish, including zebrafish and fugu, exists as a single protein-producing unit that only encodes for a CKI.
source: The Cdkn2a/b locus of teleost fish, including zebrafish (Danio rerio) and fugu (Takifugu rubripes) (Gilley and Fried, 2001), exists as a single protein-producing unit that only encodes for a CKI.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilley and Fried, 2001

claim: Arf is thought to be the product of a genetic duplication caused by either an insertion or transposition into the Cdkn2a/b locus.
source: Arf is thought to be the product of a genetic duplication caused by either an insertion or transposition into the Cdkn2a/b locus (Gil and Peters, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gil and Peters, 2006

claim: None of the highly regenerative species for which genomes have been completely sequenced possess an ortholog of Arf.
source: Of the highly regenerative species for which genomes have been completely sequenced, none possess an ortholog of Arf (Figure 1A) (Flicek et al., 2014; Karolchik et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Flicek et al., 2014 and Karolchik et al., 2014, and by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The earliest documented ortholog of Arf exists in the chicken genome.
source: The earliest documented ortholog of Arf exists in the chicken genome (Kim et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2003

claim: The human ARF promoter (736 bp) is active in HeLa cells and in zebrafish cell lines (ZF4 and ZKS).
source: These assays confirmed that the 736 base pair (bp) promoter is active in HeLa cells and in zebrafish lines.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: ARF:GFP expression was not detected in zebrafish embryos at 24, 48, and 72 hpf by immunofluorescence.
source: We were unable to detect ARF:GFP expression in the embryo head, body, or tail by wide field epi or confocal immunofluorescence indicating that the ARF promoter is silent at these developmental stages (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: In situ hybridization confirmed that ARF is silent or minimally expressed during development, including the developing tail fin region.
source: The in situ hybridization results confirmed the immunofluorescence analysis and indicate that ARF is silent or minimally expressed during development, including the developing tail fin region.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C

claim: ARF:GFP was induced and highly expressed in the blastema of regenerating adult fins.
source: In stark contrast to development, ARF:GFP was induced and highly expressed in the blastema of regenerating adult fins.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D

claim: GFP colocalized with Msxb and PCNA expressing cells in ARF:GFP fins after amputation.
source: GFP was specifically detected in ARF:GFP fins after amputation, and GFP colocalized with Msxb and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) expressing cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: GFP was not detected in the surrounding epithelium of regenerating fins.
source: GFP was not detected in the surrounding epithelium.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The ARF promoter is active in at least a subset of Msxb + blastema cells.
source: This observation indicates that the ARF promoter is active in at least a subset of Msxb + blastema cells.
evidence: Inferred from colocalization data shown in Figure 1D

claim: GFP signal in the regenerate was first detected at 12 hpa, peaked at 48 hpa, and then declined to undetectable levels within 6 days.
source: GFP signal in the regenerate was first detected at 12 hr postamputation (hpa), peaked at 48 hpa, and then declined to undetectable levels within 6 days (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E and images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: GFP expression mirrored proliferative changes during fin regeneration.
source: GFP expression mirrored proliferative changes, suggesting that ARF detects and responds to high proliferative signaling in the regenerate.
evidence: Supported by correlation between GFP expression and EdU incorporation shown in Figure 1E

claim: GFP was undetectable in healing epithelial wounds without blastema formation.
source: As expected, GFP was detected in the forming ventral blastema. However, GFP was undetectable in the healing wound.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: ARF specifically senses and responds to signals particular to the regeneration environment that differ from those present during wound healing or developmental organogenesis.
source: These distinct ARF responses to development and to the two different forms of injury indicate that ARF specifically senses and responds to signals particular to the regeneration environment that differ significantly from those present during wound healing or in the highly proliferative environment of developmental organogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from differential ARF activation patterns shown in Figures 1B, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: p-Rb1 levels were relatively low in uninjured adult fins.
source: Whereas p-Rb1 levels were relatively low in uninjured adult fins, a modest increase was detected in 72 hpf embryos.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: A modest increase in p-Rb1 was detected in 72 hpf embryos.
source: Whereas p-Rb1 levels were relatively low in uninjured adult fins, a modest increase was detected in 72 hpf embryos.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 2 dpa regenerates contained a dramatic increase in p-Rb1 levels despite stable levels of total Rb1 and total E2f1.
source: However, 2 dpa regenerates contained a dramatic increase in p-Rb1 levels despite stable levels of total Rb1 and total E2f1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Immunostaining revealed a dramatic increase in p-Rb1 staining during regeneration.
source: Similar to Western blot analysis, immunostaining revealed a dramatic increase in p-Rb1 staining during regeneration (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B

claim: p-Rb1 hyperphosphorylation and GFP were co-expressed in cells specifically localized within the blastema.
source: Co-immunostaining for GFP, and Msxb confirmed that p-Rb1 hyperphosphorylation and GFP were co-expressed in cells specifically localized within the blastema.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B

claim: ARF is bound by E2f1 specifically during regeneration.
source: We found that in contrast to the state before amputation, ARF is bound by E2f1 specifically during regeneration as is tk1 but not tk1- (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Binding of the ARF promoter by E2f1 was enriched over sixfold relative to non-amputated controls and the tk1- control.
source: The ChIP assay showed that binding of the ARF promoter by E2f1 was enriched over sixfold relative to non-amputated controls and the tk1- control.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Despite modestly increased p-Rb1 levels in 72 hpf embryos, no increase in E2f1 binding of the ARF promoter was observed.
source: Despite the modestly increased p-Rb1 levels in 72 hpf embryos, which correlated with enrichment of E2f1 at the tk1 promoter, no increase in E2f1 binding of the ARF promoter was observed.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The ARF promoter responds strongly and specifically to suprathreshold free E2f1 levels present during regeneration as opposed to other physiological contexts.
source: This finding suggests that the ARF promoter responds strongly and specifically to suprathreshold free E2f1 levels present during regeneration as opposed to other physiological contexts.
evidence: Inferred from differential E2f1 binding patterns shown in Figure 2C

claim: Human ARF localized to the nucleolus and co-localized with Mdm2 in zebrafish cells.
source: Confocal imaging showed that human ARF localized to the nucleolus and co-localized with Mdm2 in zebrafish cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Elevated Tp53 levels were observed in approximately 40% of ARF transfected zebrafish cells.
source: Elevated Tp53 levels were readily observed in approximately 40% of ARF transfected cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: When induced with an hour long, 37°C heat shock, ARF is robustly expressed in the fin 3 hr later.
source: Immunostaining showed that when induced with an hour long, 37°C heat shock, ARF is robustly expressed in the fin 3 hr later (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3

claim: ARF protein shows a rapid decrease almost to baseline at 6 hr after heat shock induction.
source: Western blot confirmed induction of ARF protein expression and also showed a rapid decrease almost to baseline at 6 hr (Figure 3), in accordance with the known 6 hr half-life of the human protein (Sherr, 2006).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3 and citation to Sherr, 2006

claim: ARF expression caused significant inhibition of fin regeneration as evidenced by reduced regenerate length and area.
source: ARF expression caused significant inhibition of fin regeneration as evidenced by reduced regenerate length and area; WT regenerates measured 1.2 ± 0.13 mm in length and 5.4 ± 1.3 mm2 in area compared with hs:ARF regenerates, which measured 0.84 ± 0.13 mm in length and 3.0 ± 0.76 mm2 in area, a reduction of approximately 30% (p<0.001) and 45% (p<0.001), respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by quantification and images shown in Figure 4B

claim: After the heat shock regimen ended, fin regeneration resumed to reach full length by 14 dpa.
source: After the heat shock regimen ended, fin regeneration resumed to reach full length by 14 dpa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: When previously heat-shocked hs:ARF fins were reamputated and allowed to regenerate in the absence of heat shock, the fins regenerated equally as well as WT fins.
source: When previously heat-shocked hs:ARF fins were reamputated and allowed to regenerate in the absence of heat shock (Figure 4A, bottom), the fins regenerated equally as well as WT fins (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C

claim: ARF inhibits fin regeneration in a reversible manner and its continued expression is required for regeneration suppression.
source: This indicates that ARF inhibits fin regeneration in a reversible manner and that its continued expression is required for regeneration suppression.
evidence: Inferred from data shown in Figure 4C

claim: ARF expression during regeneration promotes Tp53 protein upregulation.
source: The induction and stabilization of p53 and induction of cdkn1a transcripts by ARF showed that ARF impacts p53 functions in vivo in fish regenerates.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: ARF expression during regeneration promotes tp53 transcript upregulation.
source: Significant increases in tp53 (N=5 fins, p<0.05) and cdkn1a (N =5 fins, p<0.01) were observed with ARF expression.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: ARF expression during regeneration promotes cdkn1a transcript upregulation.
source: Significant increases in tp53 (N=5 fins, p<0.05) and cdkn1a (N =5 fins, p<0.01) were observed with ARF expression.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: There was no difference in regenerate length or area in hs:ARF; tp53M214K/M214K fish despite ARF expression.
source: Using the same amputation and heat shock regimen, we analyzed fin regeneration and found no difference in regenerate length or area despite ARF expression in tp53 mutant fish (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Treatment of hs:ARF fish with 5 μM PFTα increased regenerate length by 50% and area by approximately 75% compared with carrier-treated controls.
source: Treatment of hs:ARF and WT fish with 5 μM PFTα and heat shock increased hs:ARF regenerate length from 0.44 ± 0.04 mm to 0.66 ± 0.08 mm, an increase of 50% (p<0.01), and area from 1.8 ± 0.7 mm2 to 3.2 ± 0.5 mm2, an increase of approximately 75% (p<0.05), compared with carrier-treated controls.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Fin regeneration of WT fish was not affected by PFTα treatments.
source: Fin regeneration of WT fish was not affected by PFTα treatments (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Treatment of WT fish with 5 μM nutlin3a reduced fin regenerate length by 30% and area by 40%.
source: Treatment of WT fish with 5 μM nutlin3a reduced fin regenerate length from approximately 0.65 ± 0.1 mm to 0.45 ± 0.1 mm, a decrease of 30% (p<0.01), and area from 4.7 ± 1.2 mm2 to 2.8 ± 0.7 mm2, a reduction of 40% (p<0.05) (Figure 5C, left), phenocopying the fin regeneration inhibition phenotype of induced hs:ARF fish (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C

claim: ARF functions through Tp53-dependent mechanisms to inhibit fin regeneration.
source: Together, these experiments show that ARF functions through Tp53-dependent mechanisms to inhibit fin regeneration, and also demonstrate the importance of active suppression of Tp53 by Mdm2.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5

claim: EdU incorporation was significantly higher in WT fin regenerates compared with hs:ARF regenerates at 2, 4, and 6 dpa with the greatest difference occurring at 2 dpa (171%).
source: EdU incorporation was significantly higher in WT fin regenerates compared with hs:ARF regenerates at all time points examined with the greatest difference occurring at 2 dpa (171%, p<0.001) (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The incidence of apoptosis increased with ARF expression at all time points examined with the greatest difference occurring at 2 dpa (210%).
source: When the percent of TUNEL + cells in WT and hs:ARF regenerates was compared, the incidence of apoptosis increased with ARF expression at all time points examined with the greatest difference occurring at 2 dpa (210%, p<0.01) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Either a single heat shock or 24 hr of heat shocks at 4 dpa significantly reduced the number of cycling cells in the regenerate.
source: The results showed that either a single heat shock or 24 hr of heat shocks at 4 dpa significantly reduced the number of cycling cells in the regenerate, demonstrating a direct effect of ARF on the regenerating cell population (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 6C

claim: ARF:ARF transgenic fish are viable, develop normally, and have no overt size or morphological differences when compared with age- and sex-matched WT counterparts.
source: We observed, however, that ARF:ARF transgenic fish are viable, develop normally, and have no overt size or morphological differences when compared with age- and sex-matched WT counterparts (Figure 7A, right).
evidence: Supported by images shown in Figure 7A

claim: There was no effect of the ARF:ARF transgene on survival during early embryogenesis compared with WT fish.
source: In agreement with the predictions of ARF:GFP experiments, there was no effect of the ARF:ARF transgene on survival during early embryogenesis compared with WT fish (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: ARF was not detected in ARF:ARF embryos.
source: We also did not detect ARF expression in embryos, as expected given our findings with ARF:GFP fish (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: Upon heat shock, hs:ARF embryos exhibited drastically reduced survival that was associated with high levels of ARF expression throughout the embryo.
source: Upon heat shock, hs:ARF, but not WT clutches, exhibited drastically reduced survival that was associated with high levels of ARF expression throughout the embryo (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by survival and immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: ARF expression is very poorly tolerated by developing embryos.
source: This finding indicates that ARF expression is very poorly tolerated by developing embryos and clearly implies that in ARF:ARF fish, ARF is not activated significantly during development to affect normal developmental growth and organogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from survival data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: When ARF:ARF fins were injured, ARF was detected in the regenerate.
source: When ARF:ARF fins were injured, ARF was detected in the regenerate (Figure 7B), and the pattern of expression was similar to GFP expression in ARF:GFP regenerates at the same time point (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B

claim: ARF:ARF regenerates were 55% and 44% shorter and 70% and 55% smaller in area than WT regenerates in two independent transgenic lines.
source: In all, ARF:ARF regenerates were 55% (p<0.001) and 44% (p<0.001) shorter and 70% (p<0.001) and 55% (p<0.001) smaller in area than WT regenerates, and anatomical fin defects persisted 1 month after amputation (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantification and images shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: ARF expression persisted in ARF:ARF fins but not WT fins at 6 dpa.
source: ARF expression persisted in ARF:ARF fins but not WT fins at 6 dpa (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A), a time point at which GFP in no longer observed in regenerated ARF:GFP fins, suggesting ongoing regeneration attempts in ARF:ARF fins.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A

claim: Tp53, tp53, and cdkn1a expression increased with ARF expression in ARF:ARF fins at 4 dpa.
source: Tp53, tp53, and cdkn1a expression increased with ARF expression in ARF:ARF fins at 4 dpa (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B

claim: Treatment of ARF:ARF fins with 5 μM PFTα rescued fin regeneration.
source: As in hs:ARF fish, treatment of ARF:ARF fins with 5 μM PFTα rescued fin regeneration (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C

claim: ARF:ARF fin regenerates had significantly fewer proliferating cells than WT fin regenerates at 2, 4, and 6 dpa with the largest difference observed at 4 dpa (81%).
source: Similar to hs:ARF fins, ARF:ARF fin regenerates had significantly fewer proliferating cells than WT fin regenerates at all time point assessed with the largest difference observed at 4 dpa (81%, p<0.001) (Figure 7—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3D

claim: ARF activation is specific to regenerating tissue.
source: These results confirm that ARF activation is specific to regenerating tissue and show that the magnitude of activation is sufficient to inhibit regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from data shown in Figures 7B and 7C

claim: The presence of a functional human ARF gene in fish results in a diminished regenerative capacity, including absence of epimorphic regeneration, without significantly affecting other major physiological or developmental characteristics.
source: Thus, the presence of a functional human ARF gene in fish results in a diminished regenerative capacity, including absence of epimorphic regeneration, without significantly affecting other major physiological or developmental characteristics.
evidence: Inferred from data shown throughout Figure 7

claim: The core mammalian tumor suppressor ARF senses regeneration signals and specifically responds to negatively alter the proliferative balance in the zebrafish blastema, greatly perturbing regeneration.
source: We found that the core mammalian tumor suppressor ARF senses regeneration signals and specifically responds to negatively alter the proliferative balance in the zebrafish blastema, greatly perturbing regeneration.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple experiments shown in Figures 1-7

claim: This study provides the first in vivo experimental evidence that evolution of tumor suppressors can negatively impact solid tissue regeneration potential.
source: Our findings provide the first in vivo experimental evidence that evolution of tumor suppressors can negatively impact solid tissue regeneration potential.
evidence: Summary claim based on all experimental findings

claim: ARF is a critical tumor suppressor in mammals.
source: The evidence that ARF is a critical tumor suppressor in mammals (Sherr, 2006, Sharpless, 2005), but opposes regeneration functions (Sharpless and DePinho, 2007), suggests that the selective pressure that has driven the evolution of ARF has primarily enhanced tumor suppression either at the expense of or in the absence of regeneration pressures.
evidence: Supported by citations to Sherr, 2006 and Sharpless, 2005

claim: ARF opposes regeneration functions.
source: The evidence that ARF is a critical tumor suppressor in mammals (Sherr, 2006, Sharpless, 2005), but opposes regeneration functions (Sharpless and DePinho, 2007), suggests that the selective pressure that has driven the evolution of ARF has primarily enhanced tumor suppression either at the expense of or in the absence of regeneration pressures.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharpless and DePinho, 2007 and experimental data from this study

claim: Cdkn1a (p21) knockout mice possess a somewhat enhanced ability to regenerate solid structures such as pinnae.
source: It is notable, however, that Cdkn1a (p21) knockout mice do possess a somewhat enhanced ability to regenerate solid structures (Heber-Katz et al., 2013; Clark et al., 1998) such as pinnae, which lack the complex tissue structure of a digit, but nonetheless, demonstrate that alteration of cellular growth control mechanisms can impact regeneration.
evidence: Supported by citations to Heber-Katz et al., 2013 and Clark et al., 1998

claim: Active repression of ARF is important to maintain stem cell function.
source: Moreover, the importance of active repression of ARF to maintain stem cell function (Molofsky et al., 2005), and of ARF reduction to facilitate dedifferentiation (Pajcini et al., 2010) have been documented.
evidence: Supported by citations to Molofsky et al., 2005 and Pajcini et al., 2010

claim: ARF reduction facilitates dedifferentiation.
source: Moreover, the importance of active repression of ARF to maintain stem cell function (Molofsky et al., 2005), and of ARF reduction to facilitate dedifferentiation (Pajcini et al., 2010) have been documented.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pajcini et al., 2010

claim: ARF is not developmentally expressed in the majority of tissues in the mouse.
source: Moreover, prior observations that ARF is not developmentally expressed in the majority of tissues in the mouse (Gromley et al., 2009; Zindy et al., 2003) support the fidelity of the promoter used in this study.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gromley et al., 2009 and Zindy et al., 2003

claim: ARF represents an unusual departure from the paradigm that tumor suppressors function in regeneration as they do in normal development.
source: Although the majority of tumor suppressors probably function in regeneration as they do in normal development, the findings of the present study indicate that ARF represents an unusual departure from that paradigm in that the properties that cause it to respond specifically to tumorigenesis also cause it to distinguish regeneration contexts from developmental ones.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing differential ARF activation in development versus regeneration

claim: ARF is a barrier to mammalian epimorphic regeneration because it interprets the regeneration context as similar to tumorigenesis.
source: Our findings with respect to ARF strongly suggest that it is a barrier to mammalian epimorphic regeneration because it interprets the regeneration context as similar to tumorigenesis.
